t: A life insurer spends ₹8 lakh on new office furniture that will be used for several years. How should this outlay be classified?
e: Expenditure that creates an asset giving benefit over more than one accounting period is capital expenditure and is shown in the balance sheet, with only depreciation charged to revenue each year.

t: A machine costs ₹10,00,000, has an estimated residual value of ₹1,00,000 and a useful life of 9 years. Under the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation?
e: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost minus residual value) divided by useful life = (10,00,000 minus 1,00,000) / 9 = ₹1,00,000 per year.

topic: Life Assurance Business: Important Types of Life Assurance Policies
t: Which type of life assurance policy pays the sum assured only if the life assured dies within the policy term and pays nothing on survival to the end of the term?
e: Pure term assurance provides death cover only for a fixed term with no survival benefit, which is why its premium is the lowest. Endowment and money back policies carry survival benefits and whole life covers death whenever it occurs.

topic: Life Assurance Business: Important Types of Life Assurance Policies
t: In a unit linked insurance plan (ULIP), which amount is used to purchase units credited to the policyholder's unit account?
o: The premium net of the premium allocation charge
e: The premium allocation charge is deducted upfront and the balance is invested in units at the prevailing NAV. Mortality and other charges are then recovered periodically by cancelling units.

t: A yearly-mode premium on a life policy falls due on 10 June. Up to which date can the premium be paid within the grace period?
e: The grace period is 30 days for yearly, half-yearly and quarterly modes (15 days for monthly mode), so the premium due on 10 June may be paid up to 10 July without the policy lapsing.

t: A policyholder pays the renewal premium three months before its due date. How should the life insurer treat this amount in its books until the due date?
o: As a current liability (premium received in advance)
As premium income of the current year
As a direct addition to the life fund
As a deposit held with IRDAI
e: Since premium is income only when due, an amount received before the due date is held as premium received in advance under current liabilities and transferred to income on the due date.

t: A life insurer earned profit after tax of ₹600 crore on an average net worth of ₹4,000 crore. Its return on equity is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Return on equity = Profit after tax / Net worth = 600 / 4,000 = 15%, indicating the return generated for shareholders on their capital.

t: A life insurer reports gross premium of ₹1,200 crore, reinsurance premium accepted of ₹15 crore and reinsurance premium ceded of ₹60 crore. What is the net premium earned to be carried to the Revenue Account?
e: Net premium = Gross premium + Reinsurance accepted minus Reinsurance ceded = 1,200 + 15 minus 60 = ₹1,155 crore, which is the figure shown in Schedule 1.

t: According to IRDAI accounting norms for life insurers, a death claim is to be accounted for at which point?
o: When the claim amount is actually paid
When the claim is intimated to the insurer
When the claim is admitted by the claims committee
On the policy anniversary following death
e: Death claims are accounted on intimation, so that the liability is recognised as soon as the insurer becomes aware of the event. Maturity and survival benefits, by contrast, are accounted when due.

t: Policy benefits that remain unclaimed with a life insurer for more than ten years are required to be transferred to which fund?
o: Policyholders' Protection Fund of the Life Insurance Council
e: Under the Senior Citizens' Welfare Fund Rules, amounts lying unclaimed with insurers for more than ten years must be transferred to the Senior Citizens' Welfare Fund, though the claimant can still seek them for a further period.

t: A life assured dies during the grace period of a participating endowment policy with sum assured ₹5,00,000 and accrued bonus ₹60,000. The unpaid premium in respect of the current period is ₹12,000. What amount is payable as the death claim?
e: The policy is in force during the grace period, so the full sum assured plus bonus (₹5,60,000) is payable, less the unpaid premium that was due, giving ₹5,48,000.

t: Under the IRDAI (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations, if a life insurer delays settlement of a claim beyond the prescribed period, interest is payable to the claimant at what rate?
e: The regulations require interest at a rate two percent above the bank rate prevailing at the beginning of the financial year in which the claim is reviewed, for the period of delay.

t: Which section of the Insurance Act, 1938 restricts the expenses of management that a life insurer may incur?
e: Section 40B deals with limitation of expenses of management in life insurance business, with the actual limits laid down by IRDAI regulations. Section 40C covers general insurance, Section 41 prohibits rebates and Section 45 relates to repudiation of policies.

t: A life insurer's actual expenses of management for a year exceed the limit allowable under the IRDAI Expenses of Management regulations. How must the excess be treated?
o: Carried forward as deferred expenditure to the next year
Debited to the policyholders' Revenue Account
Borne by shareholders by charging it to the Profit and Loss Account
Adjusted against the Fair Value Change Account
e: Expenses beyond the allowable limit cannot be loaded on policyholders; the regulations require the excess to be borne by the shareholders through the Profit and Loss (shareholders') Account.

t: In the financial statements of a life insurer prescribed by IRDAI, commission paid to agents and intermediaries is disclosed in which schedule?
e: Schedule 2 shows commission on first year, renewal and single premiums separately, and is distinct from Schedule 3 which covers operating expenses related to insurance business.

t: Which statement about Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) under Section 115JB and life insurance companies is correct?
o: MAT applies to life insurers at 15% of book profit
MAT does not apply to income from life insurance business
MAT applies only to foreign life insurers
MAT replaces the 12.5% rate under Section 115B
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 115JB(5A) provides that MAT provisions do not apply to income accruing from life insurance business, which is taxed under Section 115B at 12.5%.

t: Under the IRDAI Investment Regulations, what is the minimum percentage of the Life Fund (non-linked, non-pension) that must be invested in Central Government securities?
e: The pattern of investment requires not less than 25% of the Life Fund in Central Government securities, and not less than 50% in Central Government, State Government and other approved securities taken together.

t: Under the investment pattern for the Life Fund, the maximum that may be placed in Other Investments (investments not qualifying as approved investments) is:
e: Other investments are capped at 15% of the Life Fund. Approved investments (other than the mandated government and infrastructure categories) may go up to 35%.

t: A life insurer holds listed equity shares in its non-linked policyholders' fund. Unrealised appreciation on these shares at the balance sheet date is credited to:
o: The Revenue Account as investment income
e: Listed equities are carried at fair value, but unrealised gains or losses are taken to the Fair Value Change Account in the balance sheet and are not available for distribution, unlike realised gains which pass through the Revenue Account.

t: Which section of the Insurance Act, 1938 governs the manner in which the controlled fund of a life insurer is to be invested?
e: Section 27A (read with Section 27) prescribes how the assets of a life insurer are to be invested and empowers IRDAI to specify the pattern. Section 64V deals with valuation of assets and liabilities.

t: A life insurer's Life Fund is ₹20,000 crore, of which ₹2,400 crore is invested in infrastructure and housing. What additional investment in this category is required to meet the regulatory minimum?
o: Nil, the minimum is already met
e: The regulations require at least 15% of the Life Fund in housing and infrastructure, i.e. ₹3,000 crore. The existing ₹2,400 crore (12%) leaves a shortfall of ₹600 crore.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: In the format prescribed for life insurers, the Revenue Account (Form A-RA) is also described as the:
e: Form A-RA is the Policyholders' Account or Technical Account, capturing premium, investment income, benefits, expenses and change in valuation reserves. The Shareholders' Account (Form A-PL) is the Non-technical Account.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: Which statement is prepared in Form A-BS under the IRDAI (Preparation of Financial Statements and Auditor's Report) Regulations for life insurers?
e: Form A-BS is the Balance Sheet; Form A-RA is the Revenue Account and Form A-PL is the Profit and Loss Account. The suffix identifies the statement.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: The item Funds for Future Appropriations in a life insurer's balance sheet represents:
o: Surplus whose allocation between policyholders and shareholders has not yet been determined
Provision for outstanding claims not yet paid
Reserve for unexpired risks on short-term policies
e: Funds for Future Appropriations (FFA) hold surplus, mainly from participating business, that has not been allocated either as bonus to policyholders or as transfer to shareholders at the balance sheet date.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: How is the cash flow statement of an Indian life insurer required to be prepared under the IRDAI financial statement regulations?
o: Either direct or indirect method at the insurer's option
It is not required for insurance companies
e: The regulations stipulate that the cash flow statement (Receipts and Payments Account) be prepared under the direct method as per AS 3, which shows gross cash receipts and payments by category.

topic: Final Accounts: Revenue Account and Balance Sheet
t: A life insurer's participating fund shows a distributable surplus of ₹900 crore for the year. Under the IRDAI norms on distribution of surplus, what is the maximum that can be transferred to shareholders?
e: Shareholders' share of surplus in the participating fund is capped at 10% (the 90:10 rule), so at most ₹90 crore goes to shareholders and at least ₹810 crore is for participating policyholders.

t: Which budgeting approach requires every activity to be justified afresh from a zero base each period rather than building on the previous year's figures?
e: Zero-based budgeting ignores past allocations and requires managers to justify each decision package from scratch, which helps eliminate inefficient or obsolete activities.

t: A firm has total assets of ₹50 lakh and liabilities to outsiders of ₹30 lakh. Using the accounting equation, what is the owners' capital?
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Assets = Liabilities + Capital, so Capital = 50 minus 30 = ₹20 lakh. This equation reflects the dual aspect concept.

t: What distinguishes a flexible budget from a fixed budget?
o: It is prepared for exactly one level of activity
It is revised every month regardless of activity
It is prepared only for capital expenditure
It recasts costs for different levels of activity by separating fixed and variable costs
e: A flexible budget recognises cost behaviour and can be flexed to the actual activity level, making variance analysis meaningful; a fixed budget is static for one planned level.

t: A life insurer's branch budgeted renewal premium collection of ₹500 crore for the year, but actual collections were ₹470 crore. What is the variance?
e: Actual revenue short of budget is an adverse (unfavourable) variance: 500 minus 470 = ₹30 crore adverse, i.e. 6% below budget.

t: The embedded value of a life insurance company is best described as:
o: Adjusted net worth plus the present value of future profits from in-force business
Value of new business plus goodwill
e: Embedded value = adjusted net worth (shareholders' net assets) + value of in-force business (discounted future shareholder profits from existing policies). It excludes the value of future new business.

t: Under IFRS 17 / Ind AS 117, the unearned profit on a group of insurance contracts that is released to profit over the coverage period is called the:
e: The contractual service margin (CSM) is the component of the insurance contract liability representing unearned profit, recognised as services are provided; the risk adjustment compensates for non-financial risk.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: Which of the following Accounting Standards is specifically stated to be not applicable to insurers under the IRDAI (Preparation of Financial Statements) Regulations, 2002?
e: The regulations state that AS 13 shall not be applicable, because valuation and accounting of investments by insurers is governed by the regulations themselves. AS 3 and AS 17 apply with modifications.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: Under the IRDAI regulations, AS 17 (Segment Reporting) applies to an insurance company:
o: Only if its securities are listed on a stock exchange
Only if its turnover exceeds ₹50 crore
Irrespective of whether its securities are listed or not
Not at all, since insurers report by line of business
e: IRDAI makes segment reporting mandatory for all insurers regardless of listing, requiring segmental revenue accounts for participating, non-participating, linked, pension and other segments.

topic: Accounting Standard (Applicable to Life Insurance Companies)
t: Which Accounting Standard deals with net profit or loss for the period, prior period items and changes in accounting policies?
e: AS 5 requires separate disclosure of prior period items, extraordinary items and the effect of changes in accounting policies so that the financial statements remain comparable.

t: Non-disclosure of a material fact by the proposer makes the contract:
o: Voidable at the option of the insurer
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Breach of utmost good faith renders the contract voidable, not void; the insurer may elect to avoid it (subject to Section 45 for life).

t: The 13th month persistency ratio of a life insurer indicates:
o: The proportion of policies (or premium) still in force after the first policy year
The proportion of claims settled within thirteen months
The ratio of expenses to premium over thirteen months
The solvency position measured over thirteen months
e: Persistency measures how many policies continue to be renewed; the 13th month ratio captures retention at the first renewal and is a key indicator of sales quality and profitability.

t: A life insurer has operating expenses of ₹900 crore, commission of ₹300 crore and gross written premium of ₹10,000 crore. What is its operating expense ratio (excluding commission)?
e: Operating expense ratio = Operating expenses / Gross written premium = 900 / 10,000 = 9%. Including commission, the total expenses of management ratio would be 12%.

t: The conservation ratio of a life insurer is computed as:
o: Renewal premium of the current year divided by the total premium (first year plus renewal) of the previous year
Claims paid divided by premium earned
New business premium divided by total premium
Surplus divided by the life fund
e: The conservation ratio shows what portion of last year's premium base was retained as renewal premium this year, and is a measure of business retention.

t: A life insurer reports available solvency margin of ₹3,600 crore and required solvency margin of ₹2,000 crore. Which statement is correct?
o: Its solvency ratio is 0.56 and it breaches the control level
Its solvency ratio is 2.0 and it meets the control level
Its solvency ratio is 1.8 and it exceeds the control level of 1.5
Its solvency ratio is 1.5 and it exactly meets the control level
e: Solvency ratio = ASM / RSM = 3,600 / 2,000 = 1.8 (180%), which is above the IRDAI control level of 150%.

t: In which year was life insurance business in India nationalised with the formation of the Life Insurance Corporation of India?
e: The LIC Act, 1956 nationalised life insurance and LIC commenced operations on 1 September 1956 by taking over 245 companies and provident societies. General insurance was nationalised in 1972.

t: The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2021 raised the permissible foreign direct investment limit in Indian insurance companies to:
e: The 2021 amendment raised the FDI cap from 49% (set by the 2015 amendment) to 74% under the automatic route, subject to safeguards on board composition and retention of profits.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: ₹1,00,000 is invested at 8% per annum compounded annually. What will it amount to at the end of two years?
e: Future value = 1,00,000 × (1.08)^2 = 1,00,000 × 1.1664 = ₹1,16,640. Simple interest would give only ₹1,16,000.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: The primary objective of asset-liability management (ALM) in a life insurance company is to:
o: Ensure that the cash flows and duration of assets are matched with those of policy liabilities
Maximise the equity component of the investment portfolio
e: ALM aligns the timing, amount and interest sensitivity of assets with long-term policy liabilities so that changes in interest rates or liquidity needs do not endanger solvency.

t: Deduction for life insurance premium under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act is available up to an overall limit of:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹1,50,000 aggregate for all 80C items; premium qualifies only up to 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012.

topic: Application of Financial Management Concepts in the Insurance Industry
t: New business strain in life insurance refers to:
o: The loss arising from policies lapsing in the first year
The strain from actual mortality exceeding expected mortality
The cost of reinsurance on new policies
The temporary deficit arising because initial expenses and reserves exceed the first-year premium received
e: Writing new business consumes capital because acquisition costs and the initial reserve set-up exceed the first premium; this strain is recovered from future premiums and surplus.

t: Under Section 115B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, profits and gains of life insurance business are taxed at the rate of:
e: Section 115B prescribes a concessional rate of 12.5% on profits of life insurance business, computed under Section 44 and the First Schedule; other income of the company is taxed at normal corporate rates.

t: The profits and gains of a life insurance business are computed for income-tax purposes under:
o: Section 44 read with the First Schedule
e: Section 44 overrides the normal heads of income and requires insurance profits to be computed per the First Schedule, where life business profit is based on the actuarial surplus with prescribed adjustments.

topic: Anti-Money Laundering Guidelines and Prevention of Money Laundering (PML) Act
t: Under the PMLA rules, an insurer must file a Cash Transaction Report with FIU-IND for cash transactions (single or integrally connected in a month) aggregating to:
e: The CTR threshold is ₹10 lakh, covering all cash transactions of that value or a series of integrally connected cash transactions within a month exceeding ₹10 lakh.

topic: Anti-Money Laundering Guidelines and Prevention of Money Laundering (PML) Act
t: Within what time must an insurer furnish a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) to FIU-IND after concluding that a transaction is suspicious?
e: The PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules require the STR to be furnished within seven working days of the Principal Officer being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious.
